sections.label: Enhanced penalties for vulnerable victims
sections.summary: In 2019, enhanced punishments of up to twice the maximum penalties were provided for offences against vulnerable victims and those in close relationships, with increased penalties for sexual offences against minors and extended protection to minors aged 16 to 18.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: First, in 2019, we had provided for enhanced punishments of up to twice the maximum prescribed penalties for some offences committed against vulnerable victims and persons in intimate or close relationship with the offender.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Second, to better protect minors under 16, we increased the penalties for the offences of rape, sexual assault involving penetration and sexual penetration of minors where the offender was in an exploitative relationship with the minor.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Third, we extended protection to minors between 16 and 18 years of age.

sections.label: Increase for outrage of modesty
sections.summary: This was a 24% increase from 2011 to 2015, and it is proposed to raise the maximum imprisonment for outrage of modesty under section 354(1) from two to three years.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This was a 24% increase from the previous five-year period from 2011 to 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We have proposed to increase the maximum imprisonment term for OM under section 354(1) of the Penal Code from two years to three years.

sections.label: False information to public servant
sections.summary: Clause 12 amends section 182 to cover offenders who give false information intending or knowing it is likely to cause a public servant to do something he or she would not otherwise do.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Clause 12 therefore amends section 182 to cover cases where the offender gives false information intending or knowing it is likely that the false information would cause the public servant to do anything which he or she would not otherwise do.

sections.label: False information as obstruction
sections.summary: The amendment clarifies that giving false information to a public servant can amount to obstruction even without physical obstruction or threats, and the maximum imprisonment under section 186 increases from three to six months.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: The amendment makes clear that the act of giving of false information to a public servant can amount to obstruction, even if there was no physical obstruction or the use of threats.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: In addition, the maximum imprisonment term under section 186 will be increased from three to six months.

sections.label: Deception on sexually transmitted disease risk
sections.summary: Clause 28 widens the offence to cover deception about the risk of the victim contracting a sexually transmitted disease, such as a lie that the disease is not transmissible by sexual intercourse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Clause 28 widens the offence to cover deception pertaining to the risk of the victim contracting a sexually transmitted disease, for example, a lie that the disease is not transmissible by sexual intercourse.

sections.label: Definition of child abuse material
sections.summary: The definition of child abuse material and abusive material will be amended to cover images of a minor's genital region, buttocks or breasts, whether exposed or covered.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Currently, "child abuse material" and "abusive material" include material that depicts an image of a minor's breasts or genital or anal region in circumstances which reasonable persons would regard as being offensive.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: We will amend this definition to cover images of a minor's genital region, buttocks or breasts, whether exposed or covered.

sections.label: Conspiracy to murder penalty
sections.summary: Maximum imprisonment under section 115 is increased from 15 to 20 years for parity with section 512.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: For example, a person who conspires with another to murder a victim where the murder was not carried out could, depending on the facts, be just as culpable as a person who attempts but fails to commit the murder itself.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: We will therefore increase the maximum imprisonment under section 115 from 15 years to 20 years, for parity with section 512.

sections.label: Provocation partial defence scope
sections.summary: The amendment broadens the partial defence where the accused did not know and had no reason to believe the provocation was lawful.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: The amendment will broaden the scope of this partial defence so that an accused person can rely on the partial defence if he did not know and had no reason to believe that the provocation was given by anything done in obedience to the law or by a public servant in the lawful exercise of the public servant's power.

sections.label: Archaic terms and defence proposals
sections.summary: Clauses replace archaic terms with modern ones, and proposals are made on unsoundness of mind and caning age limits.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: As part of our continuing efforts to ensure that the law is more easily understood by present-day readers, clauses 11, 14, 15, 16, 32, 33 and 39 replace certain archaic terms, such as "wantonly", "maliciously", "malice" and "malignantly", with modern terms that are more easily understood and already defined in the Penal Code, such as "rashly" and "intentionally".

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: First, noting that it is intended to narrow the applicability of the defence of unsoundness of mind, I would argue that public interest may be better served to go to the other direction – to broaden the grounds for raising the defence of unsoundness of mind.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Second, in keeping with the raison d'etre of this Bill, which is to protect women, children and vulnerable persons from sexual predators, there should not be an age limit to caning as punishment.

sections.label: PCRC section 84 broadening
sections.summary: The PCRC advocated broadening section 84 to include volitional acts and allow the defence where only moral wrong was unknown.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In 2018, the Penal Code Review Committee (PCRC), in its seminal report issued in August 2018 that precipitated the amendments to the Penal Code in 2019, also advocated a broadening of section 84 of the Penal Code that would allow accused persons with serious mental illnesses to receive clinical intervention instead of being punished.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It made two points: that section 84 should be broadened to include volitional acts because "there is no good reason why the criminal law should not account for the fundamental principle that a person should not be held criminally responsible for his involuntary conduct".

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The majority of the Committee also felt it would be sufficient for an accused to be entitled to the defence of unsoundness of mind even if he knew what he did was legally wrong, so long as he did not know what he did was morally wrong, by reference to an objective standard.

sections.label: Caning age cut-off
sections.summary: Caning for serious sexual offences is subject to a bar on caning male offenders aged 50 or above, introduced in 1900.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: As is well known, sentences of caning prescribed in the Penal Code provisions dealing with serious sexual offences are subject to a requirement in the Criminal Procedure Code that a male offender of or above the age of 50 cannot be caned.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In March 2020, I highlighted in this House, that the cut-off age of 50 was first introduced in 1900.

sections.label: Repeat offender over 50 sentencing
sections.summary: A repeat offender over 50 may get a less deterrent sentence even with up to 12 months' additional imprisonment in lieu of caning.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: A repeat offender over 50 may potentially get a less deterrent sentence even after taking into account that he may get an additional term of imprisonment of up to 12 months in lieu of caning.

sections.label: Caning age cut-off for sexual offenders
sections.summary: The speaker argues this House must ensure caning for serious sexual offences is decided by medical fitness, not age, and address the 50-year cut-off.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In my respectful view, it is for this House to ensure that the caning provisions being passed as punishment for serious sexual offences continue to be fit for purpose.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: That is, whether a person can be caned or not should be determined by medical fitness, and not age.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It is this House’s duty to deal with the unintended consequence of maintaining 50 as the cut-off age for such sexual offenders.

sections.label: Section 182 amendment after High Court decision
sections.summary: The Explanatory Note and Minister of State confirm section 182 is amended in light of the High Court decision in Public Prosecutor v Chua Wen Hao.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: According to the Explanatory Note to the Bill and confirmed by the Minister of State earlier as well, section 182 is being amended in light of the High Court decision this year in Public Prosecutor v Chua Wen Hao.

sections.label: Questioning new section 182 illustration
sections.summary: The speaker notes the Chief Justice held false information causing mere inefficiency was not under section 182, and questions adding illustration (d).

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Chief Justice made clear that false information leading to a public servant simply being inefficient in carrying out his lawful duties did not come under section 182.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: That being the case, I wonder why it is necessary to amend section 182 and, in particular, to add another illustration (d) to capture the situation where false information simply leads to an inefficient use of Police resources.

sections.label: New SCDF paramedics illustration
sections.summary: A new illustration describes SCDF paramedics falsely told a lift is out of order, confirming section 186 will cover giving false information.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A new illustration is introduced, where a group of SCDF paramedics is attending to a case of heart attack in a high-rise block, intending to use the lift to the 30th floor; the paramedics are then told by the offender that the lift is out of order, which is not true, causing them to take the stairs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This new illustration confirms that section 186 too will be expanded to cover the giving of false information.

sections.label: Section 186 maximum jail term
sections.summary: The speaker questions raising section 186's maximum jail term from three to six months, matching section 177 despite differing culpability.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Giving false information to a public servant when one is under a legal duty to give information is arguably more serious than when one is not under such a duty.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This raises the additional question of why the maximum jail term under section 186 is now being brought to the same level as section 177, being raised from three months to six months, when there is a difference in culpability.

sections.label: Replacing genitals with genital region
sections.summary: Clauses 30, 31 and 34 seek to replace the term "genitals" with "genital region".

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, clauses 30, 31 and 34 seek to replace the term “genitals” with “genital region”.

sections.label: Clause 12 wording change
sections.summary: Clause 12 adds the words "or would not" after the words "ought not to".

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Clause 12 adds the words "or would not" after the words "ought not to".

sections.label: Section 182 expansion question
sections.summary: The question asks whether clause 12 expands section 182 to cover the same ground as section 177, which remains untouched.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: My question, Sir, is whether section 182 is now being expanded by clause 12 to cover the same ground as section 177, seeing as section 177 remains untouched.

sections.label: Sentencing Advisory Panel update
sections.summary: The question asks for updates on the timeline, terms of reference and composition of the Sentencing Advisory Panel announced in March 2021.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The first is with regard to the Sentencing Advisory Panel that the Minister for Law announced in March 2021 and whether the Ministry has any updates on the timeline for the setting up of the panel, the terms of reference and the composition of the panel.

sections.label: Outrage of modesty case numbers
sections.summary: Outrage of modesty cases from 2016 to 2020 were 24% higher than from 2011 to 2015, as reported on 5 March 2021.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: As mentioned by Minister Shanmugam, which was reported in The Straits Times on 5 March 2021, the number of outrage of modesty cases between 2016 and 2020 was 24% higher than from 2011 to 2015.

sections.label: Reporting platform and offender register
sections.summary: The question asks whether the Ministry will consider a reporting platform and whether Singapore has a register of sexual offenders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Will the Ministry consider setting up a platform where parents, adults and minors can easily report such perpetrators?

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Is there a register of sexual offenders in Singapore?

sections.label: Registry or self-declaration for offenders
sections.summary: The question asks whether the Ministry will consider a registry or self-declaration to keep convicted sexual offenders from working with the vulnerable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Can the Ministry consider some form of registry or self-declaration such that convicted offenders of sexual offences will not be able to work in situations where they will be exposed to the vulnerable?

sections.label: Offender registry for vulnerable protection
sections.summary: An offender registry can enhance protection for the vulnerable and flag offenders employed as teachers, tutors or school bus drivers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: While harsher sentences do act as a deterrence, we can enhance protection for the vulnerable against convicted offenders by establishing an offender registry.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: We can deter or at least be aware of such offenders when they are employed in situations where they may be exposed to the vulnerable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Such jobs may include teachers, tutors and school bus drivers.

sections.label: Criminal Law Bill amendments
sections.summary: The amendments in the Criminal Law Bill are made in light of current trends in the legal landscape.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: The amendments made in the Criminal Law Bill are in light of the current trends in our legal landscape.

sections.label: Clarification on adult offender measures
sections.summary: Clarification is sought on measures ensuring adult sexual and hurt offenders no longer threaten public safety after serving sentences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: First, I would like to seek clarification on the measures to ensure that adult offenders who commit sexual and hurt offences no longer pose a threat to public safety once they have served their sentences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This Bill will raise the maximum penalties for outrage of modesty, engaging in sexual activities in the presence of a minor and causing a minor to view sexual images.

sections.label: Enhanced punishment for outrage of modesty
sections.summary: Assault or criminal force to outrage modesty draws enhanced punishment of two to three years, but section 354(2) penalties for under-14 victims were not increased.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Anyone who assaults or uses criminal force with intent to outrage modesty would be attracting an enhanced punishment from two years to three years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: This sends a strong signal that such sexual violence cannot be condoned.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: However, under section 354(2), where the offence is perpetrated upon children under the age of 14, the penalty has not been increased.

sections.label: Rationale for section 354(2) age limit
sections.summary: The rationale is questioned for limiting section 354(2) to victims under 14 and children under the CYPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Separately, what is the rationale to limit section 354(2) to victims under 14 years of age and children as defined under the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA)?

sections.label: Raising section 354(2) penalty
sections.summary: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim suggested raising the section 354(2) penalty, but it was felt unnecessary at this stage.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim suggested that we should raise the penalty for section 354(2).

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We felt that it was not necessary at this stage.

sections.label: No reason to raise age limit
sections.summary: The assessment is that there is no reason to raise the age limit, and courts can impose up to 12 months' additional imprisonment in lieu of caning.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Again, our assessment is that there is no reason to raise the age limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Where an offender is not eligible for caning, as Mr Murali Pillai and Members of this House will know, the Court can still impose an additional imprisonment term of up to 12 months, in lieu of caning, if it assesses that there is a need to do so.

sections.label: Sentencing Advisory Panel details pending
sections.summary: The terms of reference and composition of the Sentencing Advisory Panel will be provided in due course after details are firmed up.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked for an update on the setting up of the Sentencing Advisory Panel with regard to the terms of reference and its composition.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We will provide, on the formation of the Sentencing Advisory Panel, the terms of reference and its composition in due course, after the details are firmed up.

sections.label: Raising section 186 maximum term
sections.summary: Raising the maximum imprisonment term for section 186 to six months aligns its penalties with section 177(1) to cover conduct of similar blameworthiness.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The proposed raising of the maximum imprisonment term for section 186 to six months is to align the penalties with that of section 177(1) so that they can potentially cover conduct of similar blameworthiness.

sections.label: Penalties for section 376A penetration
sections.summary: Sexual penetration under section 376A is punishable with up to 10 years' imprisonment and/or a fine for victims aged 14 to 16, and up to 20 years with possible caning if below 14.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: An offence of sexual penetration under section 376A of the Penal Code is now punishable with up to 10 years of imprisonment and/or a fine if committed against a victim between the ages of 14 and 16.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: However, if the victim is below the age of 14, the offence is punishable with up to 20 years of imprisonment instead and there is also a possibility of caning.

sections.label: Offences despite overseas origin
sections.summary: The offences will be committed even if the communication originated outside Singapore or the perpetrator is outside Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The offences will be committed even if the communication originated from outside of Singapore or the perpetrator is outside Singapore.

sections.label: Interventions for sexual offence inmates
sections.summary: Selected inmates who committed sexual offences receive evidence-based psychological interventions to mitigate their risks of sexual reoffending.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Selected inmates who had committed sexual offences are given evidence-based psychological interventions to mitigate their risks of sexual reoffending.

sections.label: Conditional Remission System release
sections.summary: Offenders who committed offences on or after 1 July 2014 are placed on the Conditional Remission System upon release.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Offenders who committed offences on or after 1 July 2014 are subjected to the Conditional Remission System, or CRS, upon their release.

sections.label: Mandatory Aftercare Scheme ex-offenders
sections.summary: Ex-offenders at higher risk of reoffending or needing more reintegration support may be placed on the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Ex-offenders who are at a higher risk of reoffending, or who require more support in their reintegration, may also be emplaced on the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme, or MAS.

sections.label: Screening employees working with children
sections.summary: MOE and MSF work with the Police to screen prospective employees for jobs working with children, and mandatory screening is being considered.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Agencies like MOE and MSF work closely with the Police to screen prospective employees applying for jobs working with children, such as those in licensed preschools and schools.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We are considering whether to make it mandatory that all persons employed in similar sectors working with children, be screened.

sections.label: Unsoundness of mind defence
sections.summary: Under section 84(c), an act is not an offence if the person was, by unsoundness of mind, completely deprived of power to control his actions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Under section 84(c), nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is completely deprived of any power to control his actions.

sections.label: Conjunctive requirements policy position
sections.summary: The policy position was that the requirements should be conjunctive.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Our policy position was that the requirements should be conjunctive.

sections.label: Clarifying conjunctive reading of requirements
sections.summary: The 2019 amendments clarified the legal position in favour of a conjunctive reading, and this is being made even clearer now.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Prior to the 2019 amendments, the legal position on whether a conjunctive or disjunctive reading should be applied was unclear.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We sought to clarify this in 2019 in favour of a conjunctive reading and are making it even clearer now.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Even if an accused person does not meet the threshold of unsoundness of mind under section 84, the Court will still consider the evidence on the person's mental condition in determining what the appropriate sentence should be.

sections.label: Section 304C causing or allowing death
sections.summary: Section 304C, introduced in 2019, covers persons who allowed abuse causing death, addressing cases where both deny responsibility.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Section 304 sets out the offence of causing or allowing the death of a child below 14 years of age, or a domestic worker, or a vulnerable person in the same household.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I spoke about this earlier in the House, I think, in March or perhaps earlier.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This offence deals with situations where two or more persons were in a position to cause the death of the victim, but both deny that they were the ones who caused the death.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And both parents, and sometimes, it is the step parent that denies responsibility.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This provision will cover such situations because if they did not do it, nevertheless, they knew it was happening and they had a duty to protect the child.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: With such ambiguity, a perverse result that both get acquitted on the basis that the case against neither can be proven beyond reasonable doubt, that is a travesty of justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, we introduced section 304C in 2019 to allow us to deal with persons and not just persons who abused a victim and caused his/her death, but also persons who stood by and allowed the abuse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: In my delivered speech, I did not make reference to a case of a 49-year-old malingering to get over the age of 50 so as to avoid the sentence of caning.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: Notwithstanding that, I appreciate the point he makes that any cut-off age that we would have, would not completely resolved the issue.
